slide.title: Where Does AI Help?
slide.body: Row of five simple icons: chat bubble, sorting tray, headset, open book, bar chart, with a person icon in the middle. Small tag: AI for Customer Experience and Support · Lesson 1.

scenes.on_screen_text: New questions, or the same ones?
scenes.voiceover: Think about the last busy day on your support team. How many questions were new? And how many had you already answered a hundred times? AI is useful for that second group. Today we see where it helps, and where people must stay in charge.

slide.title: Where AI Helps in Customer Support
slide.body: AI for Customer Experience and Support · Lesson 1 of 12

scenes.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to AI for Customer Experience and Support. In this first lesson, we look at the five most common ways AI helps a support team.

slide.title: Use 1: Chatbots
slide.body: Answers customer questions in a chat window · website, app or messaging service · customers write in their own words, no fixed menu. Side strip shows five numbered slots, slot 1 highlighted.

scenes.voiceover: AI in support is not one single tool. It is a group of uses. The first use is chatbots. A chatbot answers customer questions in a chat window, on a website, in an app or in a messaging service. Modern chatbots use a language model, so customers can write in their own words.

slide.title: Use 2: Ticket triage
slide.body: Incoming message (email / form / chat) → AI adds four tags: Topic · Urgency · Language · Mood → arrow to one of three team queues.

scenes.voiceover: The second use is ticket triage. When a message arrives by email, form or chat, AI reads it and adds labels: the topic, the urgency, the language and the customer's mood. Then the ticket goes to the right team.

scenes.stock_query: support agent with headset reading computer screen
scenes.voiceover: The third use is agent assistance. Here AI does not talk to the customer. It helps the agent. It can suggest a reply, summarise a long conversation, find the right help article, or translate a message. The agent reads, edits and decides what to send.

slide.title: Use 4: Knowledge base
slide.body: A shelf of labelled help articles at the bottom as the foundation; the other four uses (chatbots, triage, agent assistance, analytics) sit on top of it.

scenes.voiceover: The fourth use is the knowledge base, your collection of help articles, policies and guides. AI can help write and update articles, find gaps, and search them to answer questions. A good knowledge base supports almost everything else.

slide.title: Use 5: Support analytics
slide.body: Many small ticket and review cards → AI groups them into themed piles; the biggest pile is labelled 'New login page'. Caption: Fix the cause, not only the questions.

scenes.voiceover: The fifth use is support analytics. AI reads thousands of tickets, reviews and survey comments, and groups them by theme. For example, many complaints this month mention a new login page. Now managers can fix the cause.

slide.title: AI and people
slide.body: Left, AI: repeated work · predictable questions · speed and consistency. Right, People: judgement · empathy · unusual cases. Bottom banner: Faster answers without losing the human touch.

scenes.voiceover: All five uses share one goal: faster, more consistent answers, without losing the human touch. AI is good at repeated, predictable work. People are better at judgement, empathy and unusual cases. A good team uses both.

scenes.stock_query: busy hospital reception desk with visitors
scenes.voiceover: Here is a picture to keep in mind. Think of a busy hospital reception. A sign on the wall answers, where is the pharmacy? A receptionist sends patients to the right department. A nurse prepares notes for the doctor. And the doctor makes the important decisions.

slide.title: Who plays which role?
slide.body: Four figures in a row: Sign, Receptionist, Nurse (all tagged AI, teal) and Doctor (tagged Person, highlighted).

scenes.voiceover: AI in support can play the sign, the receptionist and the helpful nurse. But the difficult decisions still belong to a person.

scenes.stock_query: customer support team working in modern office
scenes.voiceover: Now let's meet three hypothetical companies. First, a telecom company in Morocco. Youssef leads a support team that receives many messages in Arabic, French and English, mostly about bills and mobile data.

slide.title: Youssef's triage
slide.body: Messages in Arabic, French, English → AI labels topic + language → queues: Bills · Mobile data. A separate red arrow: 'Lost or stolen phone' → straight to a person (possible fraud).

scenes.voiceover: The team adds AI triage. Each message is labelled by topic and language, and sent to the right queue. Agents now start each ticket already knowing both. But messages about a lost or stolen phone always go straight to a person, because they can involve fraud.

slide.title: Linh's chatbot
slide.body: Chat window with two questions answered from help articles: 'Where is my order?' · 'How do I return an item?' Third message 'My product is damaged' → chatbot offers to connect a person.

scenes.voiceover: Second, an online shop in Vietnam that sells home appliances. Linh runs its support. Customers often ask, where is my order, and how do I return an item? Linh sets up a chatbot that answers these two questions from the help articles. When a customer wants to complain about a damaged product, the chatbot offers a person.

scenes.stock_query: contact centre agent typing reply on laptop
scenes.voiceover: Third, a small airline in Mexico. Mariana manages its contact centre. Flight changes involve rules, fees and stressed travellers. So AI never answers customers directly. It suggests a reply and a summary, and the agent checks the fare rules and edits before sending.

slide.title: Three companies, three choices
slide.body: Morocco telecom → Triage (fraud cases to a person). Vietnam shop → Chatbot for two simple questions. Mexico airline → Agent assistance only.

scenes.voiceover: Notice that each company chose a different use, based on its own questions and risks.

scenes.on_screen_text: Start with simple, frequent, low-risk questions
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to start by asking, how can we replace agents with a chatbot? That leads to frustrated customers. A better question is, which of our questions are simple, frequent and low risk? Start there, and grow step by step.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Five uses: chatbots, triage, agent assistance, knowledge bases, analytics. 2. AI for frequent, predictable, low-risk; people for judgement, empathy, unusual cases. 3. Start from your questions and risks, not a tool.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, the five main uses of AI in support are chatbots, ticket triage, agent assistance, knowledge bases and support analytics. Second, AI works best on frequent, predictable, low-risk questions. People handle judgement, empathy and unusual cases. Third, start from your own questions and risks, not from a tool.

scenes.on_screen_text: Next: How AI Assistants Answer Questions
scenes.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will list the ten questions your team receives most often. You will mark each one: AI can answer, AI can help an agent, or a human must handle it. Keep your list for later. In the next lesson, we look at how AI assistants answer questions. See you there.
